title: The Coastal Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Portugués Costero
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.

spans.t: The Coastal Way starts where the Portuguese Way starts, at the Sé, the cathedral of Porto, and ends where every Way ends, in Santiago de Compostela. In between it chooses the sea. It follows the Atlantic north through the fishing and beach towns of Portugal, crosses into Spain by boat across the Minho on its usual line, and in Galicia runs along cliffs and inlets to Baiona and Vigo. At Redondela it meets the other Portuguese road, and the last four days are the same for both. The CaminoPlus catalog gives the length as ~260 km. The twelve walking days of this book add up to ~272 km, and the chapters say why the figures differ.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this is your Camino, what each of the twelve days asks of you, where the road joins its neighbours, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, in three chapters, and the two chapters on other ways in and out and on the Compostela rule.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. Each day says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way". You can decide the rest later.
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally. The boat across the Minho is the clearest case: whether it runs, and when, is a question for the day.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
It is also not a second copy of
The Portuguese Way
, the book in this series about the Central route. Where the two roads share the ground, from Redondela to Santiago, this book gives the days in short and points you there.
Every distance carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate. Where something depends on the season or the day, the book says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
The road has several names: the Coastal Way in English, the
Caminho Português da Costa
in Portuguese, the
Camino Portugués de la Costa
in Spanish; the app's catalog says
Costero
Caminho
and
Camino
both mean "way". The greeting between pilgrims is
Buen Camino
in Spanish and
bom caminho
in Portuguese. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a card you have stamped along the way; a stamp is a
sello
in Spanish and a
carimbo
in Portuguese. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. A
ría
is a long sea inlet.
Pack lightly, carry something against wind and sun, and take your time.
Bom caminho.
Where it starts and ends

The Coastal Way starts at the Sé of Porto, as the Central route does, and ends at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. In Portugal the route that the government has certified passes through Porto, Matosinhos, Maia, Vila do Conde, Póvoa de Varzim, Esposende, Viana do Castelo, Caminha, Vila Nova de Cerveira and Valença. In Galicia the Xunta de Galicia, the regional government, describes the coastal route as entering at A Guarda, "after crossing the mouth of the River Miño", then passing Oia, Baiona and Vigo to join the Portuguese Way at Redondela. After that it is the same road through Pontevedra, Caldas de Reis and Padrón.
How long is it?
Nobody agrees, and that tells you how this road is built.

items.t: The CaminoPlus catalog gives ~260 km from Porto to Santiago. Wikipedia gives the same ~260 km for the Portuguese Way from Porto.
The Xunta gives ~163 km for the Galician part, from A Guarda to Santiago. The leaflet's legs add up to ~166 km, and one published plan counts ~151 km.

For the Portuguese part, the government order of 2022 that certifies the route, and the national tourism authority, give ~138 km from Porto to Valença, in nine stages. The official portal of the ten municipalities says ~149.5 km. An official guide leaflet from the municipalities, whose file dates from 2017, marks its legs at ~29, ~27, ~26 and ~27 km from Porto to Caminha, which is ~109 km, and a further ~32 km on to Valença. The three official figures for Porto to Valença are therefore ~138, ~141 and ~149.5 km.
Published walking plans put the whole road at ~271 to ~280 km.

spans.t: Part of the gap is variants: a traditional line, a seaside line on boardwalks, and three ways into Spain. Part is where each source starts and stops counting. The twelve days of this book follow the leaflet's legs in Portugal and the Xunta's stage pages in Galicia, and add up to ~272 km on foot, plus the boat. Treat every figure as a good guide, not a measurement.
The twelve days

items.t: Day 1: Porto to Vila do Conde, ~29 km
Day 2: Vila do Conde to Esposende, ~27 km
Day 3: Esposende to Viana do Castelo, ~26 km
Day 4: Viana do Castelo to Caminha, ~27 km
Day 5: Caminha to Oia, by boat and ~17 km on foot
Day 6: Oia to Baiona, ~19 km
Day 7: Baiona to Vigo, ~27 km
Day 8: Vigo to Redondela, ~16 km
Day 9: Redondela to Pontevedra, ~18 km
Day 10: Pontevedra to Caldas de Reis, ~23 km
Day 11: Caldas de Reis to Padrón, ~19 km
Day 12: Padrón to Santiago de Compostela, ~25 km

spans.t: The rounded figures add up to a kilometre more than the ~272 km total.
Where it meets its neighbours

The Confraternity of St James says the Coastal route follows the Central one out of Porto as far as Padrão da Légua, then branches off towards Vila do Conde. Wikipedia puts the split "in the countryside of Vila do Conde". Either way, after the first hours you are on a road of your own.

It touches the Central route again at Valença, which the tourism authority of Porto and the North calls the meeting point of the two. That is where the route that Portugal has certified ends. The route the Xunta describes crosses to A Guarda by boat instead, and joins the Central route at Redondela, ~85 km from Santiago by the Xunta's stage figures. A later chapter sets out these joins.
What it feels like

It is a road of sea, estuaries and small rivers. Wikipedia describes a seaside version that follows beach boardwalks, and pictures a way of ~1.5 km over the dunes at Ofir. The Confraternity calls the Portuguese coast "an interesting if undulating journey", with mixed farms and pine and eucalyptus woods behind the shore. In Galicia the Xunta describes cliffs, Cape Silleiro and the Ría de Vigo, then mussel rafts on the inner ría near Redondela. It rates the Galician part Medium-Low overall.
Why it exists
The honest history is shorter than the legend, and the sources do not fully agree.

The oldest well-attested stretch is the first one. The certification text says the route partly follows the Via Veteris, named in the royal inquiries of 1258 and for centuries the chief link between Porto and Vila do Conde. North of Vila do Conde, the same text says, a very old road network is proven along the coastal plain, but pilgrims' use of the route gains prominence only from the 18th century. The official portal says much the same: the road gained weight in the modern age, above all from the 18th century, used by coastal people and by those who landed at the ports. Wikipedia dates its prominence earlier, to the 15th century and the Age of Discovery.

The Municipality of Viana do Castelo calls the Coastal Way a derivation of the Central Way, an alternative link to Galicia. The Portuguese state certified it as a Camino itinerary in February 2022, the third route to be certified, and renewed the certification in 2025. In Galicia the Xunta notes another name, the Monastic Route, from the Cistercian monastery at Oia.
Who walks it now

Wikipedia, reporting the Pilgrim's Office statistics for 2025, says the Portuguese coastal route was the third most walked route to Santiago, with 17 per cent of pilgrims. Of those who received the Compostela on it, 51 per cent started in Porto, 21 per cent in Vigo and 12 per cent in Baiona. Of all the pilgrims who started in Porto, it adds, 45 per cent went by Vigo and 55 per cent by Tui. Most finished in May and September.

Read together, those figures say that a third of the pilgrims who finish the Coastal route started in Galicia, at Vigo or Baiona, so the Galician stretch may feel busier than the Portuguese one. That is a reading of the statistics, not a promise.
How hard is it?
Not very, and not nothing. Both authorities that rate it say the same thing. The official portal of the Portuguese municipalities gives the Portuguese part a difficulty of Medium-Low (
Média-Baixa

) and an average of seven days. The Xunta rates the Galician part Medium-Low overall: five of its eight stages are Low and three, Redondela to Pontevedra, Pontevedra to Caldas de Reis and Caldas de Reis to Padrón, are Medium. The CaminoPlus catalog gives the route a 2 on its scale of 1 to 5.

There are no mountains. What makes the days demanding is length and exposure. The Portuguese days run to ~26 to ~29 km on the leaflet's figures, and the longest Galician day, Baiona to Vigo, is ~27 km on the Xunta's. Of the shore between Portecelo and Oia, the Xunta says that it is flat, with hardly any shade, and that the sea breeze takes the edge off the summer sun. The Confraternity of St James adds that the coastal route is "undulating" because it crosses several rivers. And there is traffic: on the Baiona to Vigo stage the Xunta names the C-550, a regional road, as a constant presence.
Who it suits

It suits a first-time walker who has trained a little and wants a Camino with a clear shape: a start at a cathedral, a long run beside the sea, a boat across a border river, an arrival at another cathedral. Twelve days with a rest day or two fit inside a fortnight, and published plans cut the road at many different towns, so a day can be shortened.
It suits people who love the sea and can live with weather. The wind, the sun and the rain all matter, and a wet, windy day on an open shore asks more than the kilometres suggest.

It suits people who want company in the second half. The Office statistics, as Wikipedia reports them, show a third of those who finish the Coastal route starting in Vigo or Baiona, and from Redondela the road is shared with the Central route.
Who might choose another
If you want mountains, forest and silence, look elsewhere. The Original Way, in this series, climbs through the mountains of Asturias, and the French Way crosses the Pyrenees and the Meseta.
If you would rather have an inland road of old bridges and old towns, the Central route is
The Portuguese Way
, in this series. If you want a much longer coast,
The Northern Way
follows the north of Spain for ~820 km in the catalog. If you want the end of the land, the walk from Santiago to Finisterre and Muxía is a short one of its own.
If you hope to find the Atlantic empty in July, think again. The Confraternity says the coast is a popular holiday area that can become crowded in summer, with pressure on services and accommodation.
Questions worth asking yourself

items.t: Can you walk ~25 km on a hard surface, two or three days in a row, with your pack?
Does a day in wind and sun, with little shade, sound like an adventure or a trial?
Do you want the whole road from Porto, or the Galician coast from A Guarda or Vigo?
Are you comfortable with a plan that depends on a small boat?
What do you want from the walk: sport, solitude, the sea, a rest, prayer, a promise kept? Every answer is a good one, and the road does not ask.

spans.t: If most of your answers are yes, and the others are "we shall see", you are ready for the next chapter.

A road beside the sea is a road beside the weather. The Confraternity of St James describes northern Portugal and Galicia as a changeable maritime climate, where westerly winds bring generous rain, hence "Green Portugal" and "Green Spain". Everything below is a pattern, not a forecast. The figures are averages from stations at Porto airport, Viana do Castelo, Vigo airport and Santiago, as Wikipedia reports them. The Viana figures are older (1981 to 2010 for temperature, 1971 to 2000 for rain), and the Vigo and Santiago stations stand inland and high, so the shore itself may differ.
The seasons
Spring.

The Confraternity calls spring a rewarding time, cool, with fresh growth. It is also wet: in April the rain is ~96 mm at Porto, ~118 mm at Viana and ~150 mm at Vigo. Carry a proper rain jacket and a plan for wet feet.
Summer.

The Confraternity warns that summer can be hot and humid, and that the coast is crowded in the peak holiday months. The averages are mild: in July the mean daytime high is ~24 °C at Porto airport, ~26 °C at Viana, ~25 °C at Vigo and ~25 °C at Santiago. The averages hide the extremes: the record highs are ~38.6 °C at Porto airport, ~39.5 °C at Viana, ~40.8 °C at Vigo airport (7 August 2016) and ~39.4 °C at Santiago. Rain is scarce, ~17 mm in July at Porto and ~40 mm at Vigo. The Pilgrim's Office statistics, as Wikipedia reports them, say that most pilgrims finish the Coastal route in May and in September.
Autumn.

The Confraternity says early autumn is regarded as fairly dry and settled. By October the rain has returned: ~149 mm at Porto, ~208 mm at Vigo and ~214 mm at Santiago, and November is wetter still at Vigo, ~236 mm.
Winter.

Mild and damp. The mean daytime high in January is ~14 °C at Porto and ~12 °C at Vigo and Santiago, with lows of ~5 to ~6 °C. The trouble is rain and short days: January brings ~151 mm at Porto and ~222 mm at Vigo.

Over the whole year the rain grows as you go north: ~1,150 mm at Porto, ~1,470 mm at Viana, ~1,530 mm at Santiago and ~1,700 mm at Vigo, which Wikipedia calls the rainiest city in Galicia, with rain of 1 mm or more on ~126 days a year.
Wind

The sources read for this book give no wind speeds. They do say where the wind matters. The Confraternity names westerly winds. Wikipedia says the beaches near Porto are windier and cooler than the land inland. The Xunta says the sea breeze eases the summer sun beyond Portecelo. Expect wind on the open stretches, and read the forecast for wind as well as rain.
Daylight and the clock

At the winter solstice there are about nine hours of daylight at Porto and at Vigo, and about fifteen at the summer solstice (computed for the cities, not looked up). The clocks add a twist: mainland Portugal keeps Western European Time and Galicia Central European Time, so your watch jumps forward an hour as you cross the border. By the local clock, the December sun rises at about eight in Porto and about nine in Vigo, and sets at about ten past five and just after six. In June it rises at about six and about seven, and sets at about ten past nine and about a quarter past ten. In December, plan to be indoors by five in Portugal and six in Spain.
A month, in a line each

items.t: March and April:
cool, fresh and wet.
May and June:
mild, highs of ~20 to ~25 °C, long days; May is one of the two months when most pilgrims finish.
July and August:
warm and dry, crowded on the coast; start early.
September:
warm, the rain returning, and the other busy month.
October to February:
wet, with the shortest days.

spans.t: Holy Year and checking
Wikipedia lists the next Jacobean Holy Years as 2027 and 2032, years in which the cathedral's Holy Door is opened. If you plan to arrive in 2027, plan early and ask the Pilgrim's Office.
Before any date, look for diversions, closures, fire and heat warnings, and the boat across the Minho. A path can change between this book's date and your walk.
The credencial
The
credencial

is your pilgrim's passport, and you need one before the first stamp. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says the official model is a cardboard card of sixteen concertina-folded pages, with boxes for the stamps. You can ask for it in person at the Office or at institutions the cathedral has authorised: parish churches, associations of friends of the Way, pilgrim hostels, confraternities. The Office lists where, and it is worth looking before you leave home.

The Office gives the credencial two practical purposes: access to the hostels of the Way, and proof when you ask for the Compostela. It adds that the credencial "does not generate any rights". Stamps are normally collected where you sleep, and also in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. The Office describes a digital credential too, as a phone app. Ask the Office what it accepts, and carry the paper card in any case.
Getting there

The Confraternity of St James says you can fly into Lisbon, Porto, Vigo or Santiago and use public transport from there. Wikipedia says the airport of Vigo lies ~12 km east of the city, and that Vigo has railway stations with direct connections to Porto. The Confraternity adds a regular bus between Santiago and Porto, of about four hours' journey, which makes it possible to fly into and out of the same city. Timetables change, so check the current ones when you plan your return.
Choosing your start
Where you begin sets the length of your walk. On this book's figures, which are the day figures of the next chapters added up:

items.t: From Porto:
twelve days, ~272 km, the whole road, beginning at the cathedral, the Sé.
From Viana do Castelo:
nine days, ~190 km, which keeps the boat, the Galician coast and the arrival.
From A Guarda, after the boat:
eight days, ~163 km, the Xunta's own figure for its coastal route.
From Vigo:
five days, ~101 km by the Xunta's stage figures.

spans.t: Add a rest day or two, and a day each to travel there and back, and the Porto start is a little over two weeks. If you are choosing a start with the Compostela in mind, read the chapter on the rule first and ask the Pilgrim's Office. No starting town in this book is a guarantee.
Training

Nobody needs to be an athlete. The best preparation is also the dullest: walk, in the shoes and with the pack you will carry, on a hard surface, two or three days in a row, building up to your longest planned day, ~29 km on this road. A few weeks of regular walking will do more than any programme.
Shoes and feet

The surfaces vary: the sources mention boardwalks, paved paths, dirt tracks and old stone paths. Look for shoes with a cushioned sole, a grippy tread for wet boards and paving, and a little room in the toe box, because feet swell as the day goes on. Break them in before you leave. Two pairs of socks, changed at lunch, are a cheap defence against blisters. Treat a hot spot when you feel it, not when it has become a blister. If something hurts in a way that grows and does not fade, rest it, and see a doctor.
Packing

Pack light, and then lighter. The essentials are plain: a rain jacket, because this is a green coast; a windproof layer, because beaches are often windier and cooler than the land inland; a hat, sun protection and a water bottle, because stretches of the shore have little shade; a small first-aid kit for feet; a head torch and earplugs for shared rooms; and something dry to sleep in. A phone with an offline map is a good tool and a poor single plan, so know your next town before the battery is low.
Money, language and the clock
Portugal and Spain both use the euro. Carry some coins and small notes for small purchases. Prices are not in this book; the people you meet will tell you what things cost.

Portuguese is spoken in Portugal. In Galicia there are two official languages, Galician and Spanish, and you will meet Galician on signs and in place names such as Oia, Baiona and A Guarda. Pilgrims need little:
bom dia
("good morning" in Portuguese),
obrigado
(a man says thank you) or
obrigada
(a woman does), and in Galicia
grazas
or
gracias

Remember the clock. Mainland Portugal keeps Western European Time and Galicia Central European Time, one hour ahead. Your phone will change at the border, and your plans for the boat should change with it.
Emergencies
112 is the European emergency number and works in Portugal and in Spain. Keep it in your head, not just in your phone.
The character of these days

Four days take you out of a big city and north along the Portuguese shore to the mouth of the Minho. They are towns of the sea (Vila do Conde, Póvoa de Varzim, Esposende, Viana do Castelo, Caminha), each with a river or an estuary to cross.

A note on the figures. This book found no official stage table for the Portuguese part that it could read. The day lengths follow the legs marked on an official guide leaflet of the ten municipalities (its file dates from 2017), and published plans differ from them by several kilometres, as each day says. The road also has more than one line, so a distance depends on the line. Treat every figure as a good guide, not a measurement.
Day 1: Porto to Vila do Conde (~29 km)

You start at the Sé, and the Confraternity of St James says that the Central and Coastal routes alike spend their first day walking through the urban and industrial sprawl of Porto. That is the honest summary. If that does not appeal, the Confraternity describes a different start, the Litoral, which the chapter on other ways sets out.

The traditional line passes Matosinhos, where Wikipedia says the monastery of Leça do Balio, dated 1180, was known for the help it gave pilgrims, and then the countryside around Maia. The certification text names the monasteries of Leça do Balio and of Moreira da Maia among the places that testify to pilgrimage along the route. It also says that the way into Vila do Conde partly follows the Via Veteris, the old road of the royal inquiries of 1258, which was for centuries the chief link between the two towns. So this is the oldest, best-documented stretch of the whole road.

The leaflet marks ~29 km. Published plans cut the day differently: one stops at Labruge, ~25 km out; others run on past Vila do Conde to Póvoa de Varzim, ~37 to ~40 km from Porto. Vila do Conde is where the leaflet ends the first day. Wikipedia dates its Monastery of Santa Clara to 1318 and says the church of Azurara, by the river, was rebuilt in 1502 to commemorate the pilgrimage of King Manuel I.
Day 2: Vila do Conde to Esposende (~27 km)

The way goes through Póvoa de Varzim, where Wikipedia mentions a small chapel of St James, dated 1582, on the square, and a fishermen's quarter of the 18th century. It is also a town with a sobering sea story: Wikipedia records that on 27 February 1892 seven fishing boats were wrecked in a storm just off the shore and 105 fishermen died. Boardwalks run along the beach here, and Wikipedia pictures one at Santo André.

Esposende lies on the Cávado. Wikipedia says the crossing is now made at Fão, on a bridge of 1892, where barges once ran from Barca do Lago. It pictures a way of ~1.5 km over the dunes at Ofir and a pine wood at Fão.

The leaflet marks ~27 km to Marinhas, on the Esposende side, a little beyond the town. If you stop in Esposende itself, the day is shorter and the next one longer. Published plans give ~21 km from Póvoa de Varzim to Esposende and ~24.5 km from Póvoa to Marinhas.
Day 3: Esposende to Viana do Castelo (~26 km)

This is the day of the Neiva and the Lima. You cross the Neiva and come to Castelo de Neiva, where the certification text records a church of St James consecrated in the 9th century, and the Municipality of Viana do Castelo calls it the oldest consecrated to the apostle outside Spanish territory.

The leaflet marks ~26 km from Marinhas to Viana. One published plan says ~21 km from Marinhas, another ~24 km from Esposende; the road has more than one line here, and the differences are real. Viana do Castelo waits across the Eiffel bridge over the Lima, which Wikipedia says carried the railway, reaching the town in 1878, to a design by Gustave Eiffel. The Municipality points to the Hospital Velho, a medieval pilgrims' hostel, and the sanctuary of Santa Luzia stands above the city on its hill, begun in 1904 according to Wikipedia.
Day 4: Viana do Castelo to Caminha (~27 km)
The Municipality of Viana describes the way out of the city through Areosa and Carreço, past carved rocks, farm buildings, chapels and wayside crosses, to Afife, the convent of Cabanas and the old
cividade
of Afife, where Viana's part ends. Wikipedia describes the
cividade

as a settlement site of the Castro culture, occupied up to Roman times. The leaflet and one published plan agree on ~27 km, and another plan stops at Vila Praia de Âncora, ~19 km from Viana, to make two shorter days.

Caminha sits on the Minho estuary, about two kilometres from the Atlantic, says Wikipedia, and its old keep became the town's clock tower in the 17th century. The Mother Church dates from the 16th. The estuaries of the Minho and the Coura form a protected landscape, which Wikipedia describes as wetlands, sandbanks and reed beds that attract birds, above all in winter. From here the road goes into Spain, by one of three ways, which the next chapter sets out.
Check before you go:
diversions and path closures, and the state of the boardwalks after storms.

chapters.title: Across the Minho and the Galician coast: Days 5 to 7

spans.t: The character of these days

Three days take you across a border by water and along the coast of southern Galicia: cliffs, a lighthouse, a fortress, then the long ría of Vigo with its beaches and its city. The lengths and descriptions, unless another source is named, are those of the Xunta de Galicia's stage pages for its coastal route. The English pages of the Xunta read like translations and differ from the Spanish in places, so this book read the Spanish originals for every figure and warning. Other sources differ by a kilometre or two.
The crossing

The Xunta says the coastal route enters Galicia at A Pasaxe, in A Guarda, "after crossing the mouth of the River Miño", and that the walker has said goodbye to Portugal at Caminha. The Confraternity of St James says a boat crosses the estuary, and Wikipedia says the contemporary crossing is by ferryboat from Caminha to A Guarda. The official leaflet marks the leg at ~4 km.

In April 2022 the Xunta announced a boat service for pilgrims and residents between A Guarda and Caminha, with two boats, one electric, and a dedicated electric boat planned for that summer. That was a press release, not a timetable. This book cannot tell you whether a boat runs on your day, or at what hour. A road that depends on a boat depends on the boat. Ask in Caminha the day before, and read the chapter on other ways in and out for the alternative.
Day 5: Caminha to Oia (~17 km on foot, plus the boat)

A Guarda to Oia is rated Low, ~16.7 km, ~3 h 20 min, though its first section, ~10.8 km to Portecelo, is rated Medium-High. The leaflet breaks the day further on, at Mougás, a little beyond Oia, ~24 km from A Guarda.

A Guarda grew on the lower slopes of Mount Santa Trega, a viewpoint over the Atlantic and Portugal and the site of a pre-Roman fortified settlement, occupied from the 1st century BC to the 1st century AD. It was declared a National Historic-Artistic Monument in 1931, and some of the hill's stones carry petroglyphs. From the top you look down on the mouth of the Miño, especially beautiful at low tide and at sunset, with rushes, cormorants and ducks on the marsh.

From Portecelo the route follows the coast with the ocean on your left. This section is flat, with hardly any shade, and the sea breeze lessens the summer sun. It leads to the monastery of Santa María de Oia, on the shore. Its front, in the austere Cistercian style, dates from the late 12th century; the church has baroque altarpieces; and in the mid-18th century, the Xunta says, the monks beat off an attack by a Turkish fleet. The Xunta also says the monastery was being restored, so check what you can visit. It gives the route its other name, the Monastic Route.
Day 6: Oia to Baiona (~19 km)

Rated Low, ~18.6 km, ~3 h 45 min. You leave the fishing village of Oia and walk along the foot of the cliffs, past the lighthouse of Cape Silleiro, opened in 1866 and the chief landmark for ships on the south side of the Ría de Vigo.
The route then climbs to Baredo by the old royal path,
vereda real
, and some kilometres later reaches the castle of Monterreal, a hotel today. Its walls held off the English corsair Francis Drake, who landed in 1585, and a path runs around it beside the sea.

Behind the castle lies Baiona. On 1 March 1493 it was the first port in Europe to learn of the discovery of America, from the caravel La Pinta, captained by Martín Alonso Pinzón. The ría of Vigo begins here, sheltered by the Cíes Islands, the heart of the Illas Atlánticas National Park, which you can reach by boat from Baiona.
Day 7: Baiona to Vigo (~27 km)
The longest day in Galicia: ~26.8 km, ~5 h 25 min, rated Low. Its four sections are ~4.8, ~4.2, ~9 and ~8.9 km, which are the places to split it.

You leave Baiona past the historic fountain of O Pombal and cross a Romanesque bridge over the Groba at Sabarís. The bridge at A Ramallosa is also Romanesque, with ten arches; the Xunta says it may stand on a Roman one. It marks the mouth of the Miñor river, a marsh of great ecological richness. In Nigrán you pass country houses and stone crosses, and at Panxón the Templo Votivo do Mar, by the architect Antonio Palacios. The whole stage has fine white sand beaches and, the Xunta says, a mild climate for most of the year.

Take care on this day. The regional road, the C-550, is a constant presence. For the end, the Xunta recommends the river path beside the Lagares from Samil beach, with its wetlands. An alternative through the Coia district is closer to the old tradition but, says the Xunta, spoilt by large housing developments and too much traffic. Vigo is Galicia's largest city, with close to 300,000 inhabitants and a fishing and container port.
Check before you go:
the boat across the Minho, access to the monastery at Oia, and the state of the path at Vigo.
The character of these days
One day of coast remains, the walk from Vigo to Redondela, and then four days on the road that the Central route shares.
The Portuguese Way

, in this series, walks that road day by day from the other side; here you get each day in short. The lengths and descriptions are, again, those of the Xunta's coastal stage pages. Its Central pages differ from these by up to ~0.4 km on some of the same days (~25.2 km against ~24.8 km on the last one), which shows how soft such figures are.
Day 8: Vigo to Redondela (~16 km)

Rated Low, ~16.3 km, ~3 h 10 min. In Vigo the way passes the Paseo de Alfonso XII, by the olive tree that is the city's symbol, near a surviving stretch of the old entrance to the walled town. It goes down to the O Berbés quarter and by A Pedra, known for its restaurants and the oysters of the ría. On Rosalía de Castro Street the Xunta points to the Salinae site, an underground museum of Roman saltworks.

Then comes the longer part, ~10.1 km, through Paradela, Parada, Trasmañó, Rande and Portela. Redondela is where the coastal route meets the inland Portuguese route. It has railway viaducts of the 1870s, a church of Santiago that Archbishop Gelmírez consecrated in 1114, and each May the Festa do Choco, a cuttlefish festival.
Day 9: Redondela to Pontevedra (~18 km)

Rated Medium, ~18.2 km, ~4 h 35 min. Leaving Redondela you pass the chapel of As Angustias and the parish of Cesantes, and the Ría de Vigo opens on your left. The Spanish page puts it to the west; the English page says east, which does not match the Spanish. In the middle of the ría are the islands of San Simón and San Antón, and under the water lie the galleons of the Battle of Rande of 1702. In the distance Rande Bridge rises above the mussel rafts.

At Arcade the way crosses the medieval Sampaio Bridge over the Verdugo, where the municipality of Pontevedra begins, mid-bridge, and goes on along old stone paths, with sections of the Roman road Via XIX, such as the climb of A Brea Vella de A Canicouva. It reaches Pontevedra past the shrine of the Virxe Peregrina and on into the historic centre.
The Portuguese Way
suggests Pontevedra for a rest day, and says why. It is also where the Spiritual Variant leaves the road, as the next chapter explains.
Day 10: Pontevedra to Caldas de Reis (~23 km)

Rated Medium, ~23 km, ~5 h 45 min. You cross the Lérez on the bridge of O Burgo and skirt the wetland of A Xunqueira de Alba. Three stone crosses stand along the way, one carved with St James the Pilgrim looking north to Compostela. Then comes a warning: watch the signs, because the route weaves with the N-550 road, which is always present, and a new high-speed railway has altered the landscape.
Caldas de Reis is a spa town, the
Aquae Celenis

of the Antonine Itinerary, a document of the 3rd century that records the routes of the Roman Empire. You cross a bridge to the hot spring that gives the town its name, and a medieval bridge over the Bermaña closes the day.
Day 11: Caldas de Reis to Padrón (~19 km)

Rated Medium, ~18.7 km, ~4 h 45 min. You leave Caldas by the N-550 but take a path almost at once, climbing to the church complex of Santa Mariña de Carracedo, then through the woods and old mills of Valga. In Pontecesures the bridge over the Ulla, Roman in origin and much changed, separates the provinces of Pontevedra and A Coruña. Padrón is the cradle of the Jacobean tradition, the Xunta says. In the church of Santiago is kept O Pedrón, a Roman altar stone to which a carved cross is said to have been added by the disciples of St James.
Day 12: Padrón to Santiago (~25 km)

Rated Low, ~24.8 km, ~5 h. You pass Iria Flavia, once a Roman city and an episcopal see until the 11th century, and the foundation of the writer Camilo José Cela. At the crossing of the N-550 a branch to the right takes you out of the traffic. The sanctuary of A Escravitude gives views over the valleys.
Then O Milladoiro: the
humilladoiro

, where pilgrims knelt on first seeing the cathedral. Beyond it the way crosses the Sar by the Old Bridge and offers two clearly signed ways into the city. It enters the old quarter by the Porta Faxeira and the Rúa do Franco, and the traditional entrance to the cathedral for pilgrims on the Portuguese route is through the Praza das Praterías.
Check before you go:
diversions around the N-550 and the new railway, and the Xunta's current route.

chapters.title: Other ways in and out, and other ways to split the days

spans.t: The Litoral start

The Confraternity of St James describes a way out of Porto for those who do not fancy the first day of the usual route. The Litoral starts at the cathedral like the others but drops to the promenades of the Douro estuary, follows them to the sea, and goes north on promenades and boardwalks to Vila do Conde, where it becomes the Coastal route. Wikipedia describes a similar idea as a contemporary version of the Coastal Way, pushed by German pilgrims, that keeps to the sea along beach walkways. It says this version is gaining importance because the traditional line is increasingly built up, and that bicycles are not allowed on some walkways. This book found no official length for either line, and its day figures follow the traditional one.
Three ways into Spain

At Caminha the road has a choice. The Municipality of Viana do Castelo, the tourism authority of Porto and the North and the Municipality of Vila Nova de Cerveira all say that the Coastal Way is an alternative link to Galicia and that the Minho can be crossed at three places.

items.t: Caminha to A Guarda, by boat.
This is the line the Xunta describes for the Coastal route, and the one this book follows. It joins the Central route at Redondela.
Vila Nova de Cerveira to Goián, across the river.
The Portuguese sources name it as the second crossing, and this book found nothing more about it. Ask locally.
Valença to Tui, over the bridge.

This is the end of the route that Portugal has certified: ~138 km from Porto to the border at Valença, according to the national tourism authority. From Caminha to Valença the Municipality of Vila Nova de Cerveira describes a gentle way parallel to the Minho, at the foot of Monte de Goios and the Serra da Gávea, through the old centre of Vila Nova de Cerveira, whose castle King Dinis had built to guard the crossing. The leaflet marks ~16 km to Vila Nova de Cerveira and ~16 km more to Valença; one published plan marks ~12.5 and ~14.5. The tourism authority calls Valença the meeting point of the Central and Coastal routes. From Tui you walk the Central route, which
The Portuguese Way
describes, and meet this book's road again at Redondela.

spans.t: So there are two joins, not one: Redondela, if you take the boat, and Valença and Tui, if you follow the river. The Xunta's coastal route takes the first, and the Portuguese certification the second.
The Spiritual Variant

The Confraternity describes the Spiritual Variant as relatively newly established. It begins in Pontevedra, leaves the Central route for Vilanova de Arousa on the shore of the Sea of Arousa, and from there goes by boat up the estuary to Pontecesures, where it rejoins the Central route to Santiago. The Confraternity adds that this is the way by which the body of St James is said to have travelled, in a stone boat.

The Xunta has a page for a related route, the Mar de Arousa and Río Ulla Route, which commemorates the arrival of the apostle's body by sea. It speaks of forty nautical miles from the entrance of the ría to the old Iria Flavia, and then about 25 km on foot to Santiago. The Xunta pages read for this book do not mention the Spiritual Variant by name, and this book found no official length for it. A walker on the Coastal Way reaches Pontevedra on Day 9, so the variant is open from there. A route that depends on a boat depends on the boat: ask locally before you plan around it.
Other ways to split the days

The twelve days follow the leaflet's legs in Portugal and the Xunta's stages in Galicia. They are not the only plan: the official portal says an average of seven days for the Portuguese part, the published plans read for this book count thirteen stages for the whole road, and the Xunta has eight stages in Galicia. Here are the commoner changes.

items.t: Cut Day 1.
One published plan stops at Labruge, ~25 km from Porto. Others run on past Vila do Conde to Póvoa de Varzim, ~37 to ~40 km.
Stop short on Day 4.
One published plan ends at Vila Praia de Âncora, ~19 km from Viana do Castelo, and walks on to Caminha the next morning.
Join Days 5 and 6.
The Xunta's two stages from A Guarda to Baiona come to ~35 km and divide at Oia. The leaflet puts its stop a little further on, at Mougás.
Cut Day 7.
The Xunta's sections give you places to stop: A Ramallosa, Nigrán, Coruxo.
Add a rest day.
Pontevedra is the natural place, as
The Portuguese Way
explains.

spans.t: Whatever you choose, the arithmetic is the same: twelve days, ~272 km on this book's figures, so ~23 km a day on average, less on the short days.

chapters.title: The Compostela rule, and where your start leaves you

spans.t: What the Pilgrim's Office says

The Compostela is the certificate that the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues to those who come to the tomb of the Apostle and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback. The Office asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route. On foot or on horseback, the Office asks for at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that it recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the Cathedral.

The Way may be done in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and the end of each stage, with the date. A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain. The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.
Which routes the Office recognises

The Office's pages read for this book speak of routes recognised by its own system, and say there are many traditional and recognised routes, but they do not list them. They do not mention the Portuguese Coastal route by name. The Office's own statistics, as Wikipedia reports them, count it as a route of its own. The pages also do not say how the Office treats a walk that starts on one recognised route and changes to another at a junction, as this one does at Redondela. The Xunta presents the Coastal route as a single route from A Guarda to Santiago. If any of this matters to your plan, ask the Office.
The arithmetic for this road
Here is the arithmetic, with its sources.

items.t: From Porto.

The Xunta gives its coastal route in Galicia, from A Guarda, as ~163 km. That is well over the seventy kilometres in Spain that the Office names for those who have walked a recognised route outside Spain.
From Vigo.

Add the Xunta's stage figures from Vigo to Santiago and you get ~101 km on its coastal pages, and ~101.4 km if you use its Central figures for the shared days. The Confraternity of St James calls Vigo the hundred-kilometre mark, and one published plan counts ~99 km from Vigo, just under it. The Xunta's figure is just above the hundred, and where in Vigo you begin counting, which line you walk and how the Office measures can all move it.
From Baiona.
The Xunta's stage from Baiona to Vigo adds ~26.8 km, so ~128 km; the same published plan counts ~122 km.
From Redondela.
~85 km by the same figures: under the hundred.

spans.t: None of that is a decision. The Office decides, and rules change. If you plan to start in Vigo, or anywhere near the limit, ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office lists access to "hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way" as the first practical use of the credencial, notes that hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute, and asks groups travelling with a support car, or by bicycle, to look for other shelter. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

Which hostels exist, which are open this month, whether you may book a bed and how beds are given out differ from town to town and change from season to season. This book does not list them. The Confraternity of St James warns that the coast is a popular holiday area, crowded in summer, with pressure on services and accommodation. So use the CaminoPlus app for where to sleep tonight, ask locally for tomorrow, and do not rely on one source for the long days.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and pack your rucksack in the hall, not at dawn beside sleepers.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed. Keep your valuables close.
Earplugs go a long way. Somebody will snore, and if it is you, apologise at breakfast.

spans.t: Bedbugs

are a risk in any shared bed anywhere. Check the seams of the mattress, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is not a reason to avoid hostels, only a reason to look before you lie down.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating. A good night is part of the walk.
Eating
Some places along the Way offer a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what is on it and what it costs before you sit. A set meal is a good way to eat well after a long day, and an easy way to try what the coast cooks.

The sea is the larder here, and the sources say so in their way. Wikipedia describes Póvoa de Varzim as a town of fishermen and seafarers, with a fishing history that reaches to Newfoundland. In Galicia the Xunta points to A Pedra, in Vigo, as known for its restaurants and for the oysters of the ría, and shows mussel rafts on the water at Rande. In Redondela it names the Festa do Choco, a cuttlefish festival, each May. You do not need to eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day, and eat it without a screen.
Water matters as much. Fill your bottle in each town, and carry something for lunch on the long days: Day 1, Day 4 and Day 7.
Resting
It is easy to treat the walk as a timetable to be kept. Resist that. A day of rest is part of the walk.

If you have a day to spare, there are candidates. Baiona is a place to slow down: the Xunta says the Cíes Islands, in the Illas Atlánticas National Park, can be reached by boat from there. Viana do Castelo is another, with its old hospital for pilgrims and its hill. Pontevedra is the one that
The Portuguese Way
suggests, and it lies on this road too. The last place is the end. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it deserves more than a night.
On the road, listen to your body before you listen to your plan. You are not walking to prove anything.
Feet

Look after your feet first. Take your shoes off at lunch and let your feet breathe. Change your socks. Treat a hot spot at once, before it is a blister. Boardwalks and paving are kind to nobody's feet for twenty-seven kilometres, so spend money on good shoes and time on breaking them in.
Sun and heat

The Xunta says the shore beyond Portecelo is flat with hardly any shade, and that the sea breeze lessens the summer sun. A breeze can make a hot day feel milder than it is, so wear a hat and sun protection anyway. The averages are mild but the record highs are not: ~38.6 °C at Porto airport and ~40.8 °C at Vigo airport. The Confraternity of St James warns of heat with high humidity. Start early, carry more water than you think you need, and plan the hottest hours for a café or a bench. If you feel dizzy, sick or confused, stop in the shade, drink, and ask for help; if it does not pass, call 112.
Wind and rain

The sources give no wind speeds, but they say the beaches are windier and cooler than the land inland. Carry a windproof layer, and keep your hat on a string. This is also a wet coast: Vigo averages ~1,700 mm of rain a year, on ~126 days, and the Confraternity says that in periods of low pressure the rain can be heavy and prolonged. A rain jacket and a cover for your pack are not optional, and a spare pair of dry socks in a plastic bag is the cheapest comfort on the road. Wet boardwalks and paving can be slick: shorten your stride. Rain on a long day is also a reason to take a shorter one.
Roads and paths

The Coastal Way meets roads. On the Baiona to Vigo stage the Xunta names the regional road C-550 as a constant presence, and on the shared days it warns of the N-550, which the route weaves with, and of the new high-speed railway that has altered the landscape, and asks you to watch the signs. At the crossing of the N-550 beyond Padrón it says a branch to the right takes you out of the traffic. The official portal of the Portuguese municipalities says the same in one line: for your safety, do not walk on roads with heavy traffic, and use the certified, signposted route. Where you must walk a road, the Confraternity advises you to use the indicated strip between the road and the drainage ditch.
Where there is no path, walk facing the traffic, in single file, and never in the dark. Look at the arrows at every junction.
The boat and the sea

The sea is beside you all day, and it is not a swimming pool. Do not assume there is a lifeguard or a flag on the beach. Ask locally, follow any signs, and do not swim alone or when you are tired. On the boat across the Minho, follow the instructions of the crew, and keep your phone and your credencial dry.
Border and papers

Wikipedia lists Portugal and Spain as members of the Schengen Area, so there are normally no checks between them, though member states can bring in temporary controls. Carry your passport or identity card anyway, as you should in any country.
When to stop

Stop when something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, when you are dizzy, when the weather turns, or when the light is going. A short day costs you an afternoon; a bad decision can cost you the Camino. Tell someone your plan. The emergency number is 112, in Portugal and in Spain.
Before you go, check for diversions, closures and, in summer, heat and fire warnings. A route can change between this book's date and your walk.
Why people walk

People walk this road for faith, for sport, for grief, for curiosity, for a rest from work, for a promise made to someone else. The Pilgrim's Office has its own rule for what it certifies, and the chapter on the Compostela rule gives it. The road itself asks nothing of the kind. Every reason is a good one for walking, and none of them needs to be explained to the people you meet.
What the road gives
It gives you hours with no task. For twelve days the feet, the weather, the tide and the next town set the agenda, and what you do with the quiet is yours.

This road has its own places for thinking. A shore where, the Xunta says, the mouth of the Miño is at its most beautiful at low tide and at sunset, with rushes and cormorants on the marsh. A boat you cannot hurry, which for once makes the timetable somebody else's. A coast with the ocean always on your left. A hill at O Milladoiro, the
humilladoiro
, where the Xunta says pilgrims knelt on first seeing the cathedral.

The sea is also where the old story of this road begins. The Xunta tells how ancient Christian traditions and medieval texts, above all Book III of the Codex Calixtinus, say that the body of the Apostle came to Galicia by sea, up the Ulla to Padrón, in a stone boat. You need not believe a legend to feel something when you cross the Ulla at Pontecesures. Wikipedia keeps a harder memory of the same sea: the fishermen of Póvoa de Varzim who died in the storm of February 1892. A coast is a place where people lived by the water, and sometimes lost.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, or none. They are better walked than answered.

items.t: What are you carrying that is not in your pack?
Whom would you like to have beside you on this road, and what would you say to them?
What would "enough" look like today, for your feet and for your heart?
When the wind or the weather is against you, what do you do, and what does it tell you about yourself?
What are you walking towards, and what are you walking away from? Is the second a reason to turn round, or only a reason to keep going?

spans.t: You do not have to arrive at an answer in Santiago. A better question is a fair thing to bring home.
The cathedral

The Coastal Way ends where every Way ends: at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, the reputed burial place of St James. The Xunta says the traditional entrance to the cathedral for pilgrims on the Portuguese route is through the Praza das Praterías, and that the way into the old quarter runs by the Porta Faxeira and the Rúa do Franco. Wikipedia dates the start of construction to 1075, the Praterías façade to 1103 and the great Baroque façade on the Praza do Obradoiro to 1740.

The cathedral keeps a Holy Door, which Wikipedia says is opened only in a Jacobean Holy Year, and the next Holy Years are 2027 and 2032. Wikipedia adds that in a Holy Year the great censer, the botafumeiro, is swung at all the Pilgrims' Masses. Check the cathedral's own pages for the times of the Mass: they change.
Take a moment in the square before you do anything else. Sit on the stones if you like. The arrival may be quieter or noisier than you expected; there is no right feeling.
The Pilgrim's Office and the Compostela
The
Compostela

is the certificate of your pilgrimage, and the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues it. The rule it follows is in the chapter on the Compostela rule, and it is the Office's to apply: if you are in any doubt, contact it. The Office says that both its reception service and the issuing of the Compostela are completely free.

When you arrive, bring your credencial. You also take a ticket with a QR code, which lets you follow your place in the queue on your phone. The Office warns that in times of great influx it cannot guarantee that you will receive the Compostela on the same day, so do not book a flight home for the afternoon. The Office's website gives its address and its current hours, which are not in this book because they change.
If you walked for other reasons, or are not sure that yours count, the Office also offers a separate
Certificate of Distance

, issued by the Chapter of the Cathedral. It records the kilometres you travelled, whatever your starting point. It carries a fee, and the Office gives the amount. Whichever document you ask for, the Office meets a great many people in a day. Be patient, be warm, and if you have a doubt about your credencial, ask before you queue.
The next day

Try not to leave on the morning after you arrive. A day in Santiago lets the walk settle. Wash your clothes, sleep late, and look at the old town. On the cathedral square stands the building that the Catholic Monarchs founded as a royal hospital for pilgrims; the Office says those who showed their Compostela there once had the right to stay free for three days, and that it has been a hotel since 1954. The Office adds that the cathedral is open all day, with a chapel where many people sit to think or pray.

If you still have legs and time, some pilgrims walk on to Finisterre and Muxía on the coast, ~90 km farther, a route you will find in the CaminoPlus app's list, and that has a book of its own in this series,
To the End of the Earth

. If you do not, think about the way home. The Confraternity of St James notes a bus service of about four hours between Santiago and Porto; Santiago also has an airport. Check the current times. And buy a postcard, and write to someone you walked with in your head.

The first days back are strange. The road has taught your body a rhythm of early light, one thing at a time and a short list of needs, and home does not run on it. Expect to miss the walking before you miss anything else. You may find you miss the sea most of all, or the sound of it.

Keep what you can. Walk to the shop and not to the car. Eat one meal a day without a screen, as the road suggested. Write down three things you want to remember before they blur: a boat, a face, a boardwalk. Put the credencial somewhere you will see it. A stamp is a small thing, and a full card of them is a map of a fortnight you will not live again in quite that way.

Tell the story, and listen when someone else tells theirs. Every pilgrim has one, and every one is different. If you carried a question, you need not have answered it. It may still be walking beside you.
If you want to walk again, the road has neighbours.
The Portuguese Way

, in this series, takes the inland road from Porto to the same cathedral, and you will already know its last four days. The walk from Santiago to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km in the catalog, goes on to the end of the land.
The Northern Way
is the long coast of Spain. The CaminoPlus app lists them all.
Whatever you do next, thank the people who kept the road open for you: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts, the boatmen, and the people in the villages.
Bom caminho
, and
Buen Camino
, again.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus
. The app is still in development, so look in the app for what is available on the Camino Portugués Costero today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures, the boat and the weather.

A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in CaminoPlus, or in any app other than the Office's own digital credential, is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and the fact ledger that goes with it lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Xunta de Galicia

, the regional government, on its official portal (caminodesantiago.gal): the page on the Portuguese Coastal Way and its eight stage pages, read in Spanish as well as English; the page on the Mar de Arousa and Río Ulla Route; and its press release of April 2022 on the boat across the Minho.
The government of Portugal

: the order that certifies the route (Portaria n.º 67/2022, of 2 February, in the Diário da República), the national tourism authority's page on the certification, and the pages of the tourism authority of Porto and the North.
The ten municipalities of the Caminho Português da Costa
: their official portal and guide leaflet (the file dates from 2017), and the pages of Viana do Castelo and Vila Nova de Cerveira.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the Compostela, the credencial, the Certificate of Distance and the notes on arriving.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Camino Portugués, for the routes out of Porto, the Spiritual Variant, the weather and the way there.
Wikipedia

, for history, geography, climate and the Pilgrim's Office statistics for 2025: the articles on the Portuguese Way, Porto, Vila do Conde, Póvoa de Varzim, Viana do Castelo, Caminha, Vigo, Santiago and its cathedral, the Holy Year, the Schengen Area, the number 112 and time in the two countries. The climate averages are those of the Portuguese and Spanish weather services.
Published walking plans
for the Portuguese days, compared with the leaflet. They are not named here; the ledger lists them.
Day-length figures
, computed with a standard solar calculation, and
the CaminoPlus route catalog
, for the route's name, ends, length and difficulty.

spans.t: The tourism authority's own site, Visit Portugal, could not be read when this was written, so nothing here rests on it. Stage lengths differ from one source to the next, and a few pages disagree with themselves, so every distance in this book is marked ~. This book found no official stage table for Portugal that it could read; the Portuguese figures are therefore the least certain. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.

Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, the municipalities that waymark the road, and the people in the towns and villages who point the way and say
bom caminho
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Bom caminho, Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims, in Portuguese and in Spanish.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Carimbo, sello
: a stamp in the credencial, in Portuguese and in Spanish.
Certificate of Distance
: the Pilgrim's Office document that records the kilometres you walked.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Humilladoiro
: the place where pilgrims knelt on first seeing the cathedral, in Galician.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Ría
: a long sea inlet, as at Vigo and Arousa.
Sé
: the cathedral, in Portuguese.
Vereda real
: a royal path, an old main road.
Xunta
: the regional government of Galicia.
